content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
This paper studies a parameter-efficient method for privately fine-tuning foundation models, a DP variant of the BiTFiT method. The negatives of this paper were that it has relatively low novelty in a few different ways. First, BiTFiT was already introduced in the non-private setting. Additionally, DP fine-tuning with parameter efficient methods has been investigated in both Li et al., and Yu et al.'s works from 2022. While this particular approach was not studied in those works, very similar ones were. The idea of investigating this was already suggested in at least one of these works, and thus the novelty and ideas contributed by this paper are low. The benefits were that the method was more effective in certain metrics, and the authors had a reasonably thorough investigation.

To be more direct: it is unclear whether an expert in DP ML would have their course modified by this paper. The authors emphasize that the course correction could be through the specific structure of this approach being amenable to better optimization, but this seems a bit slim/marginal for acceptance to ICLR.

Reviewer maoM had some concerns regarding the presentation of certain experimental results, which they brought up in subsequent discussion. The authors may want to address these points in a subsequent revision, either adding these experiments or discussing why they aren't appropriate.   

Note that Reviewer 7D3z did not adequately substantiate their high score in their review nor participate in the subsequent discussion, so their positive sentiment was downweighted.

content.title: Response to follow-up questions
content.comment:
Hi, happy to extend the discussion!

We did not include the adapter/compactor in Section 3.3 for two reasons: (1) Adapter/compactor are mostly transformer-specific methods, unlike the model-agnostic DP-BiTFiT that works with all models. Therefore these methods are not compatible with ResNet, VGG, etc. Especially, adapter/compactor won't fit in the right two subplots of Figure 3&4. (2) There are already dozens of points in each sub-plot. Adding adapter and compactor would require 5 points for each method and may worsen the readability.

In Section 4, the batch size is the same for full fine-tuning and BiTFiT (DP and non-DP), to make the comparison fair. However, the batch size of LoRA/Adapter/Compactor/RGP is either using the same batch size or half of it, according to the original implementation by "Large Language Models Can Be Strong Differentially Private Learners" (please see their Table 5&6 for hyperparameters). It is likely that using a larger batch size can further improves the accuracy of DP-BiTFiT, but the DP full fine-tuning could be more accurate as well. From the efficiency point of view, we would like to refer the reviewer to Figure 4 (which uses a fixed memory constraint, that is different from Figure 3 which uses the fixed batch size constraint).

Please let us know if you have more questions.

content.title: Follow-up questions
content.comment:
Dear authors,

Thank you for the response. On re-reading the paper I had two follow-up questions I was hoping you might be able to answer:

Were Adapter/Compacter included in the experiments in Section 3.3? Since these beat BiTFiT in some metrics (trainable parameters/throughput in Figure 1) it would be nice to have a complete comparison with them.

In the experiments in Section 4, is the batch size constant across all methods? I'm wondering if e.g. DP BiTFiT might perform even better if one uses, say, a fixed memory/time per epoch constraint rather than a fixed batch size, since it seems to be quiet efficient and increasing batch sizes helps with accuracy and privacy.

content.title: Thank you and our response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for liking this work! We provide point-to-point response as follows.

**Comment:** *I think the main weakness of the paper is that, as the authors mention, BiTFiT is a method introduced in a previous paper. While the authors do provide a more efficient implementation of DP-BiTFiT than the naive baseline, beyond that there is not much algorithmic novelty in the paper. That being said, the original BiTFiT paper is relatively short and doesn't provide nearly as much insight into the algorithm both theoretically and empirically as this paper, so I think this is less of a weakness and more of a lack of a certain strength.*

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for the appreciation of our insight into the BiTFiT algorithm, especially the complexity analysis and the explanation through activation-free forward propagation. If we may add, we are particularly thrilled about the similarity between DP and non-DP BiTFiT, in terms of accuracy and efficiency, whereas DP and non-DP full fine-tuning has very different time and space complexity in Table 2.

**Comment:** *However, I am hesitant to give the paper a higher score because of the limited originality. Again, I don't view this as a weakness; I still feel the paper is a quality paper ready for publication at a conference, and that having more exploratory papers such as this one to guide practice is a good thing for the community in general. However, based on the reviewing criteria, this paper may not compare favorably to a paper proposing a novel approach that also has high impact and good quality.*

**Response:** We are happy for your recognition that our paper is "a quality paper ready for publication at a conference, and that having more exploratory papers such as this one to guide practice is a good thing for the community". Thanks for the support and fair evaluation of our work!

**Comment:** *Comments for authors: Remark 4.1: I guess, the idea is that as the number of parameters increases, the fraction of them that BitFiT trains is decreasing, and so it is a relatively weaker algorithm. So if accuracy were "one-to-one" measure of how strong an algorithm is, one would expect the gap to increase with the number of parameters. But increasing accuracy generally gets more difficult as model size/baseline accuracy approaches 100\% (i.e., going from 90 to 95\% accuracy for one architecture could actually be easier than going from 98 to 99\% for a larger architecture, even though it is a "smaller gap"), and the accuracy gap decreasing could just be explained by this phenomenon. So this remark feels slightly misleading to me.*

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for this new perspective. We agree that as model size increases, BiTFiT tends to train a smaller fraction of model parameters so that non-DP/DP BiTFiT is weaker and the gap between non-DP BiTFiT and DP BiTFiT also decreases. In Remark 4.1, we are describing the gap between non-DP full and non-DP BiTFiT, or that between DP full and DP-BiTFiT. We hope this clears the reviewer's question and if not, we are happy to extend the discussion. We will add your new perspective in Remark 4.1.

**Comment:** *In contrast with the previous comment, I think Table 5 which shows DP BiTFiT starts to outperform DP full fine-tuning at large \# of parameters is one of the most interesting results of the paper and it was easy to miss on first read since this is sort of bundled in with Remark 4.1 by the text, but in my view it's really demonstrating something very different and promising. I might suggest emphasizing this more in the paper, space permitting. It makes a lot of sense, since DP suffers from curse of dimensionality, but I'm not aware of any past works that show that reducing the dimension of the optimization problem actually shows benefits in an empirical result (without assuming something like a low-rank gradient subspace), much less one where the way of reducing the dimension is so simple to describe.*

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have added "Algorithmically, we propose the Differentially Private Bias-Term Fine-Tuning (DP-BiTFiT) in Algorithm 1 that is highly accurate under DP constraint, on par with SOTA in Section 4 and even outperforming fully fine-tuned GPT2-large." in the first paragraph of Contributions section to highlight the interesting phenomenon of DP-BiTFiT on large models. It's definitely an interesting phenomenon that BiTFiT is effective and the way that BiTFiT reduces the dimension is different than low-rank assumptions. We think there might be something fundamental that merits future study in this direction.

content.title: Thank you and our response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for liking this work! We provide point-to-point response as follows.

**Comment:** *The novelty is still limited. While I acknowledge the authors’ clarification in Introduction and appreciate their efforts in the comprehensive experiments they have done, the proposed DP-BiTFiT is still a simple adaptation of BiTFiT to DP fine-tuning by adding gradient clipping and gaussian noise.*

**Response:** We agree that the novelty from an algorithmic perspective is somewhat limited. On the other hand, we would like to highlight our contribution on the insight, especially the complexity analysis that is not even reflected in the non-DP BiTFiT paper. For example, we show that DP/non-DP BiTFiT are 1.5X faster in theory than non-DP full fine-tuning. We also give the specific reason of DP-BiT being more memory-saving, which is the activation-free forward propagation in Equation (4). We would like to quote Reviewer maoM's comment: "the original BiTFiT paper is relatively short and doesn’t provide nearly as much insight into the algorithm both theoretically and empirically as this paper".

**Comment:** *Despite the training efficiency and memory usage improvement, there is some accuracy drop compared to the state-of-the-art DP fine-tuning methods. While most of the accuracy gap is subtle and acceptable, the accuracy of DP-BiTFiT in Table 7 is a bit confusing to me, where the accuracy can be as low as 1\% or 11\%, and two-phase training must be used to alleviate the issue. This raises my concern about whether the proposed DP-BiTFiT is a general framework that works for every method/model/dataset.*

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for initiating the discussion on DP-BiTFiT with computer vision tasks. Generally speaking, parameter efficient fine-tuning methods (including but definitely not only BiTFiT) are not universally applicable to all tasks. For example, last-layer fine-tuning (a.k.a. linear probing) work quite well on CV, with or without DP constraint, yet it fails on language tasks (see last sentence in the caption of Table 4): only getting 77.3\% on QNLI whereas DP-BiTFiT gets 86.5\% and DP full gets 87.9\%. Another example is that prefix-tuning, Adapter and LoRA only work on Transformers, but DP-BiTFiT works on all models.

**Comment:** *Unclear insights on two-phase training. While Table 7 has shown promising results when interpolating full fine-tuning and BiTFiT, the authors seem not to provide enough insights on why combining these methods can achieve both better efficiency as well as better accuracy. Moreover, practical and principled guidance on when and how to employ two-phase fine-tuning is missing. Additional question: Since there is some accuracy gap between DP-BiTFiT and state-of-the-art DP fine-tuning methods, have you applied the two-phase training method to close the gap or even improve the accuracy? I am willing to increase my score if my concerns are well addressed.*

**Response:** We would like to clarify that two-phase training does not achieve better efficiency: the training time of $X$+BiTFiT is longer than that of $(X-1)$+BiTFiT, and hence two-phase training is faster than DP full fine-tuning but slower than DP BiTFiT. This is empirically evaluated in Table 17 (last row) in the appendix. Accuracy-wise, we have observed on vision transformers, RoBERTa and GPT2 that larger models decrease the accuracy gap between DP full fine-tuning and DP-BiTFiT (see Remark 4.1), with DP-BiTFiT being even slightly outperforming sometimes.

As a practical guidance, we encourage the use of two-phase training when the performance of DP-BiTFiT is not satisfying, because you can always increase $X$ to achieve the accuracy of DP full fine-tuning. We haven't applied the two-phase training on NLP tasks since DP-BiTFiT is sufficiently accurate, but this could be an interesting future direction.

content.title: Thank you and here is our response
content.comment:
**Comment:** *Maybe the authors can investigate and elaborate more on when and why the proposed method would work.*

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for the comments and the appreciation of our work. We would like to elaborate 3 cases when DP-BiTFiT works best: (1) Large models: With DP or not, full fine-tuning usually gives better accuracy than parameter efficient fine-tuning. As we state in Remark 4.1 and in Table 4-6, the gap between DP-BiTFiT and DP full fine-tuning generally decreases as model size increases. (2) High dimension feature: From an efficiency perspective, DP-BiTFiT is particularly suitable for high dimension, because state-of-the-art weight-training DP algorithms use GhostClip, which has quadratic dependence on the dimension T. Also DP-BiTFiT is faster than non-DP full fine-tuning. (3) Language tasks: In our experiments, directly applying DP-BiTFiT usually give strong accuracy on NLP tasks but no so on CV tasks (see Table 7). However, this accuracy drop has been remedied by our novel two-phase training to achieve state-of-the-art results on vision tasks.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper focuses on the problem of differentially private fine-tuning of large pre-trained models, which is the most prevailing DP learning paradigm in the era of large machine models. Specifically, the authors propose to use differentially private bias-term fine-tuning (DP-BiTFiT) as a new parameter-efficient DP fine-tuning paradigm. They demonstrate that the proposed method has the following advantages: 
(1) DP-BiTFiT is model-agnostic
(2) DP-BiTFiT has its parameter efficiency around 0.1% across different pretrained models in computer vision and natural language processing. 
(3) DP-BiTFiT is computation efficient and almost removes the overhead introduced by DP, which makes the algorithm scalable to larger models with long-sequence texts or high-resolution images
(4) DP-BiTFiT matches the similar performance of state-of-the-art DP fine-tuning algorithms.
The authors conduct comprehensive studies over the model parameter efficiency, training time and space complexity, and the scalability of the DP algorithms, and empirically compare with the state-of-the-art DP fine-tuning methods on larger language models and computer vision models across different tasks under different privacy constraints.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper is clearly written and easy to follow
2. The complexity analysis and comparison is technically sound
3. The empirical experiments on memory and time complexity improvements look convincing to me

Weakness:
1. The novelty is still limited. While I acknowledge the authors’ clarification in Introduction and appreciate their efforts in the comprehensive experiments they have done, the proposed DP-BiTFiT is still a simple adaptation of BiTFiT to DP fine-tuning by adding gradient clipping and gaussian noise. 
2. Despite the training efficiency and memory usage improvement, there is some accuracy drop compared to the state-of-the-art DP fine-tuning methods. While most of the accuracy gap is subtle and acceptable, the accuracy of DP-BiTFiT in Table 7 is a bit confusing to me, where the accuracy can be as low as 1% or 11%, and two-phase training must be used to alleviate the issue. This raises my concern about whether the proposed DP-BiTFiT is a general framework that works for every method/model/dataset.
3. Unclear insights on two-phase training. While Table 7 has shown promising results when interpolating full fine-tuning and BiTFiT, the authors seem not to provide enough insights on why combining these methods can achieve both better efficiency as well as better accuracy. Moreover, practical and principled guidance on when and how to employ two-phase fine-tuning is missing.


Additional question:
Since there is some accuracy gap between DP-BiTFiT and state-of-the-art DP fine-tuning methods, have you applied the two-phase training method to close the gap or even improve the accuracy?
I am willing to increase my score if my concerns are well addressed.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well presented, except that the table is hard to interpret given that no numbers are bold.
The novelty of the paper is limited given that BiTFiT is an existing algorithm.

===
Updates after authors' response:

Overall I feel that it is a borderline paper.

I like the clarity of the writing and the comprehensive experiments to demonstrate the memory and computational efficiency improvement.

However, I share the same concerns as other reviewers that the novelty is quite limited, especially given the fact that the proposed method is not universally applicable to every task (low performance on CV tasks) and requires combining both full model fine-tuning and the proposed method to mitigate the issue. Thus the significance of the work is also reduced.

I decreased my score from 6 to 5, considering the limited novelty and significance. However, I am not against accepting the paper due to its comprehensive experiments and practical insights.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper considers applying bias-term fine-tuning (BiTFiT) to DP large model training. They describe efficient implementations of (DP)-BiTFiT and demonstrate that the time and space complexity of these implementations improves both over non-DP and DP full model training. They then give a deep empirical study of BiTFiT and its effectiveness in terms of accuracy and efficiency. They demonstrate that:
-For many problems, DP BiTFiT only needs to train ~.1-.2% of the model parameters.
-DP BiTFiT has a memory footprint and throughput that are 2-8 times better than other SOTA algorithms.
-BiTFiT's accuracy only is worse by a few percentage points in tasks where the SOTA accuracy ranges from 60-95%, when compared to full model training, even for large (100s of millions of parameters) models. Furthermore, DP BiTFiT demonstrates the same behavior and in some cases even outperforms DP full model training.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I think the main strength of the paper is that it is pretty comprehensive as an empirical exploration of the benefits of using (DP) BiTFiT for model training. The authors run many different sets of experiments, and each set of experiments is fairly comprehensive. Another strength is how well the authors present the math-based motivation for using DP BiTFiT. e.g. I thought the explanation at the bottom of Section 4 on why computing gradients of bias only is more efficient, Figure 2 visualizing back-propagation for several algorithms simultaneously, and Section 3.2 where the authors show BiTFiT has improved space and time complexity over other approaches all demonstrated a great deal of effort by the authors to make conceptually understanding the paper much more digestible. Finally, the results in the paper show a lot of promise for guiding large model training with DP in practice. e.g., I think the fact that DP FiTBiT actually improves over full model training when the number of parameters is large enough for some problems strongly demonstrates the potential of the approach. 

I think the main weakness of the paper is that, as the authors mention, BiTFiT is a method introduced in a previous paper. While the authors do provide a more efficient implementation of DP-BiTFiT than the naive baseline, beyond that there is not much algorithmic novelty in the paper. That being said, the original BiTFiT paper is relatively short and doesn't provide nearly as much insight into the algorithm both theoretically and empirically as this paper, so I think this is less of a weakness and more of a lack of a certain strength.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As mentioned in the previous section, I felt the paper was quite clear and high-quality. A lot of effort is put into maximizing the reader's understanding, and many different sets of experiments capturing comparing DP BiTFiT to full training/other approaches in many different aspects are present. The main originality of the work is the efficient implementation of DP BiTFiT; otherwise, BiTFiT is an existing algorithm and most contributions of the work are empirical.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall I weakly recommend accepting the paper. I think the paper provides a lot of intuition for a promising algorithm for practice, and may enable training much larger models with DP fine-tuning than what was previous possible, so the paper has much potential for impact. The writing and content of the paper meets the bar for acceptance in my opinion, for the reasons listed in the previous sections. However, I am hesitant to give the paper a higher score because of the limited originality. Again, I don't view this as a weakness; I still feel the paper is a quality paper ready for publication at a conference, and that having more exploratory papers such as this one to guide practice is a good thing for the community in general. However, based on the reviewing criteria, this paper may not compare favorably to a paper proposing a novel approach that also has high impact and good quality.

---
Comments for authors:
Remark 4.1: I guess, the idea is that as the number of parameters increases, the fraction of them that BitFiT trains is decreasing, and so it is a relatively weaker algorithm. So if accuracy were "one-to-one" measure of how strong an algorithm is, one would expect the gap to increase with the number of parameters. But increasing accuracy generally gets more difficult as model size/baseline accuracy approaches 100% (i.e., going from 90 to 95% accuracy for one architecture could actually be easier than going from 98 to 99% for a larger architecture, even though it is a "smaller gap"), and the accuracy gap decreasing could just be explained by this phenomenon. So this remark feels slightly misleading to me. 

In contrast with the previous comment, I think Table 5 which shows DP BiTFiT starts to outperform DP full fine-tuning at large # of parameters is one of the most interesting results of the paper and it was easy to miss on first read since this is sort of bundled in with Remark 4.1 by the text, but in my view it's really demonstrating something very different and promising. I might suggest emphasizing this more in the paper, space permitting. It makes a lot of sense, since DP suffers from curse of dimensionality, but I'm not aware of any past works that show that reducing the dimension of the optimization problem actually shows benefits in an empirical result (without assuming something like a low-rank gradient subspace), much less one where the way of reducing the dimension is so simple to describe.

content.title: Differentially private Bias-Term Only Fine-tuning of Foundation Models
content.TL;DR: We propose a parameter efficient and private fine-tuning method, that trains 0.1% of the network (only the bias terms) and substantially improves the time/space complexity.
content.abstract:
We study the problem of differentially private (DP) fine-tuning of large pre-trained models — a recent privacy-preserving approach suitable for solving downstream tasks with sensitive data. Existing work has demonstrated that high accuracy is possible under strong privacy constraint, yet requires significant computational overhead or modifications to the network architecture.

We propose differentially private bias-term fine-tuning (DP-BiTFiT), which matches the state-of-the-art accuracy for DP algorithms and the efficiency of the standard BiTFiT. DP-BiTFiT is model agnostic (not modifying the network architecture), parameter efficient (only training about $0.1\%$ of the parameters), and computation efficient (almost removing the overhead caused by DP, in both the time and space complexity). On a wide range of tasks, DP-BiTFiT is $2\sim 30\times$ faster and uses $2\sim 8\times$ less memory than DP full fine-tuning, even faster than the standard full fine-tuning. This amazing efficiency enables us to conduct DP fine-tuning on language and vision tasks with long-sequence texts and high-resolution images, which were computationally difficult using existing methods.
